source_text: Εἶτα ἐπειδὰν τὴν διὰ τῆς αἰσθήσεως πίστιν οἱ ταῦτα λέγοντες ἀπαιτῶνται, τί φασιν; Ὅτι διὰ τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς συνήθειαν πρὸς τὸν ψόφον ἐκ πρώτης γενέσεως συνεθισθέντες αὐτῷ, ἐκ πολλῆς τῆς περὶ τὸ ἀκούειν μελέτης τὴν αἴσθησιν ἀφῃρήμεθα· ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν τοῖς χαλκείοις συνεχῶς τὰ ὦτα κατακρουόμενοι. Ὧν τὸ σεσοφισμένον καὶ σαθρὸν διελέγχειν, οὕτως ἐναργῶς ἐκ πρώτης ἀκοῆς πᾶσι καταφαινόμενον, οὐκ ἔστιν ἀνδρὸς οὔτε χρόνου εἰδότος φείδεσθαι, οὔτε τῆς συνέσεως τῶν ἀκουόντων στοχαζομένου. Ἀλλὰ τὰ τῶν ἔξωθεν τοῖς ἔξω καταλιπόντες ἡμεῖς ἐπὶ τὸν ἐκκλησιαστικὸν ὑποστρέφομεν λόγον. Εἴρηται μὲν οὖν τισι τῶν πρὸ ἡμῶν, μὴ δευτέρου οὐρανοῦ γένεσιν εἶναι ταύτην, ἀλλ' ἐπεξήγησιν τοῦ προτέρου, διὰ τὸ ἐκεῖ μὲν ἐν κεφαλαίῳ παραδεδόσθαι οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς ποίησιν, ἐνταῦθα δὲ ἐπεξεργαστικώτερον τὸν τρόπον καθ' ὃν ἕκαστον γέγονε τὴν Γραφὴν ἡμῖν παραδιδόναι. Ἡμεῖς δέ φαμεν, ὅτι ἐπειδὴ καὶ ὄνομα ἕτερον καὶ χρεία ἰδιάζουσα τοῦ δευτέρου οὐρανοῦ παραδέδοται, ἕτερός ἐστι παρὰ τὸν ἐν ἀρχῇ πεποιημένον οὗτος, στερεωτέρας φύσεως, καὶ χρείαν ἐξαίρετον τῷ παντὶ παρεχόμενος. 3.4 Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεός· γενηθήτω στερέωμα ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ ὕδατος, καὶ ἔστω διαχωρίζον ἀνὰ μέσον ὕδατος καὶ ὕδατος. Καὶ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ στερέωμα· καὶ διεχώρισεν ὁ Θεὸς ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ ὕδατος ὃ ἦν ὑποκάτω τοῦ στερεώματος, καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ ὕδατος τοῦ ἐπάνω τοῦ στερεώμα τος. Καὶ πρό γε τοῦ ἅψασθαι τῆς διανοίας τῶν γεγραμμένων, πειραθῶμεν τὸ παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἀντεπαγόμενον διαλῦσαι. Ἐρωτῶσι γὰρ ἡμᾶς, εἰ σφαιρικὸν μὲν τὸ σῶμα τοῦ στερεώματος, ὡς ἡ ὄψις δηλοῖ, ῥυτὸν δὲ τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ περιολισθαῖνον τοῖς ὑψηλοῖς, πῶς ἂν ἐδυνήθη ἐπὶ τῆς κυρτῆς περιφερείας τοῦ στερεώματος ἱδρυνθῆναι; Τί δὴ πρὸς τοῦτο ἐροῦμεν; Ὅτι μάλιστα μὲν οὐκ εἴ τι πρὸς ἡμᾶς κυκλοτερὲς ὁρᾶται κατὰ τὴν ἔνδον κοιλότητα, τοῦτο ἀνάγκη καὶ τὴν ἔξωθεν ἐπιφάνειαν σφαιρικῶς ἀπηρτίσθαι, καὶ ὅλον ἀκριβῶς ἔντορνον εἶναι καὶ λείως περιηγμένον· ὅπου γε ὁρῶμεν τῶν τε λουτρῶν τοὺς λιθίνους ὀρόφους, καὶ τὰς τῶν ἀντρωδῶν οἰκοδομημάτων κατασκευὰς, ἃ κατὰ τὴν ἔνδον ὄψιν εἰς ἡμικύκλιον σχῆμα περιηγμένα, ἐν τοῖς ἄνω τοῦ τέγους ὁμαλὴν ἔχει πολλάκις τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν. Ὥστε τούτου γε ἕνεκεν μήτε αὐτοὶ ἐχέτωσαν πράγματα, μήτε ἡμῖν παρεχέτωσαν, ὡς οὐ δυναμένοις τὸ ὕδωρ κατασχεῖν ἐν τοῖς ἄνω. Ἑξῆς δ' ἂν εἴη λέγειν, τίς ἡ φύσις τοῦ στερεώματος, καὶ διὰ τίνα αἰτίαν μεσιτεύειν ἐτάχθη τῷ ὕδατι. Τὸ τοῦ στερεώματος ὄνομα σύνηθες τῇ Γραφῇ ἐπὶ τῶν κατ' ἰσχὺν ὑπερβαλλόντων τάσσειν· ὡς ὅταν λέγῃ, Κύριος στερέωμά μου, καὶ καταφυγή μου· καὶ, Ἐγὼ ἐστερέωσα τοὺς στύλους αὐτῆς· καὶ τὸ, Αἰνεῖτε αὐτὸν ἐν στερεώματι δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ. Οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἔξωθεν στερεὸν λέγουσι σῶμα τὸ οἷον ναστὸν καὶ πλῆρες, ὃ πρὸς ἀντιδιαστολὴν τοῦ μαθηματικοῦ λέγεται. Ἔστι δὲ τὸ μὲν μαθηματικὸν τὸ ἐν μόναις ταῖς διαστάσεσι τὸ εἶναι ἔχον, ἐν τῷ πλάτει, λέγω, καὶ τῷ βάθει, καὶ τῷ ὕψει· τὸ δὲ στερεὸν ὃ πρὸς τοῖς διαστήμασι καὶ τὴν ἀντιτυπίαν ἔχει. Τῇ δὲ Γραφῇ σύνηθες, τὸ κραταιὸν καὶ ἀνένδοτον, στερέωμα λέγειν, ὡς καὶ ἐπὶ ἀέρος πολλάκις καταπυκνωθέντος τῇ φωνῇ ταύτῃ κεχρῆσθαι· ὡς ὅταν λέγῃ· Ὁ στερεῶν βροντήν.
thought_title: The firmament's nature and the water above it
orientation: Basil is expounding the second day of creation, answering objections about how water can rest on the curved firmament and explaining what Scripture means by 'firmament.'
pass_a_gloss: Then whenever those who say these things are asked for the proof through sense-perception, what do they say? That because of the habit from the beginning, having become accustomed to the sound from our first origin, by much practice concerning hearing we have lost the perception; just as those in the bronze-smithies who have their ears struck continually. To refute the sophistry and rottenness of these things, which is so clearly evident to all from first hearing, is not the mark of a man who knows how to spare time, nor of one who aims at the understanding of his hearers. But leaving the things of those outside to those outside, we return to the ecclesiastical discourse. It has been said then by some of those before us, that this is not the origin of a second heaven, but an explanation of the former one, because there the making of heaven and earth was handed down in summary, but here the Scripture hands down to us in more detailed fashion the manner in which each thing came to be. But we say that since both a different name and a peculiar function of the second heaven have been handed down, this one is different from the one made in the beginning, being of a firmer nature, and providing an exceptional function to the whole. And God said: Let a firmament come to be in the midst of the water, and let it be separating between water and water. And God made the firmament; and God separated between the water which was below the firmament, and between the water above the firmament. And before touching the meaning of the things written, let us try to dissolve the objection brought forward by the others. For they ask us, if the body of the firmament is spherical, as the sight shows, and the water is flowing and slipping off from high places, how could it have been established on the curved circumference of the firmament? What then shall we say to this? That most certainly it is not the case that if something appears to us circular according to its inner cavity, this must also have its outer surface finished spherically, and the whole be exactly turned on a lathe and smoothly rounded; since indeed we see the stone roofs of the baths, and the constructions of cave-like buildings, which are rounded into a semicircular shape according to the inner appearance, often have a flat surface on the upper parts of the roof. So for this reason at least, let them neither make trouble for themselves, nor make trouble for us, as if we were unable to hold the water in the upper regions. Next it would be right to say what the nature of the firmament is, and for what reason it was ordered to mediate for the water. The name of firmament is customary for the Scripture to assign to things that excel in strength; as when it says, The Lord is my firmament and my refuge; and, I have made firm its pillars; and the saying, Praise him in the firmament of his power. For those outside call a solid body that which is dense and full, which is said in contrast to the mathematical. The mathematical is that which has its being in dimensions only, in breadth, I mean, and depth, and height; but the solid is that which in addition to the dimensions also has resistance. But it is customary for the Scripture to call the strong and unyielding thing firmament, as also it often uses this word of air that has been greatly condensed; as when it says: He who makes firm the thunder.

choices.why: Preserves both nouns as objects of refutation, matching Basil's polemical tone against the harmony-of-spheres argument.
Renders λόγος as 'discourse' to capture the homiletic context of Basil's teaching within the church.
Comparative adjective rendered literally to preserve Basil's contrast between the first and second heaven.

pass_b_english: Then, when those who say these things are asked for the proof of sense perception, what do they answer? They say that because we have been accustomed to the sound from our first origin and have grown used to it from the beginning, we have lost the perception of it through long practice in hearing it—just like people in bronze workshops who have their ears struck continually. To refute the sophistry and rottenness of this argument, which is so plainly evident to everyone at first hearing, is not the work of a man who knows how to spare time or who aims at the understanding of his hearers. But let us leave the things of outsiders to outsiders and return to the ecclesiastical discourse.

Some of those before us have said that this is not the creation of a second heaven, but a further explanation of the first, because there the making of heaven and earth was handed down in summary, while here the Scripture hands down to us in more detailed fashion the manner in which each thing came to be. But we say that since a different name and a special function of the second heaven have been handed down, this one is other than the one made in the beginning, of a firmer nature, and providing an exceptional service to the whole.

And God said, “Let a firmament come into being in the midst of the water, and let it be separating between water and water.” And God made the firmament, and God separated between the water that was beneath the firmament and between the water that was above the firmament (Genesis 1:6-7). But before we touch the meaning of what is written, let us try to dissolve the objection brought against us by others. For they ask us: if the body of the firmament is spherical, as sight shows, and water is fluid and slips off high places, how could it have been made to sit firmly on the curved surface of the firmament? What then shall we say to this? That it is not at all necessary that what appears circular to us in its inner concavity should also have its outer surface finished spherically, and be perfectly turned and smoothly rounded throughout. For we see the stone roofs of baths and the construction of cave-like buildings, which are rounded into a semicircular shape on the inner view, yet often have a flat surface on the top of the roof. So for this reason let them neither make trouble for themselves nor cause trouble for us, as though we could not hold the water in the upper regions.

Next it would be right to say what the nature of the firmament is, and for what reason it was appointed to mediate between the waters. The name “firmament” is customary in Scripture for things that excel in strength. For example, when it says, “The Lord is my firmament and my refuge” (Psalm 17:3 LXX [Hebrew 18:2]), and “I have made firm its pillars” (Psalm 74:4 LXX [Hebrew 75:3]), and “Praise him in the firmament of his power” (Psalm 150:1 LXX [Hebrew 150:1]). Those outside call a solid body something dense and full, which is said in contrast to the mathematical. The mathematical is that which has its being only in dimensions—in breadth, I mean, and depth and height—while the solid is that which has resistance in addition to the dimensions. But it is customary for Scripture to call what is strong and unyielding a firmament, as it often uses this word even of air that has been greatly condensed, as when it says, “He who makes firm the thunder” (Job 37:4 LXX [Hebrew 37:4]).

problems.why: LXX Job 37:4 is ὁ στερεῶν βροντήν, but Hebrew 37:3 is 'He unleashes his lightning beneath the whole heaven and sends it to the ends of the earth.' Hebrew 37:4 is 'After that comes the sound of his roar; he thunders with his majestic voice.' The LXX differs. The citation [Hebrew 37:3] is wrong; should be [Hebrew 37:4] or note LXX differs. Actually ὁ στερεῶν βροντήν (He who makes firm the thunder) — in Hebrew this concept appears in 37:4 about thunder, not 37:3. Hebrew 37:3 is about lightning. So [Hebrew 37:3] is incorrect; it should be [Hebrew 37:4].
problems.ruling: Hebrew 37:3 is about lightning; thunder is 37:4. The reference [Hebrew 37:3] is wrong.

fixed: The Hebrew verse for 'He who makes firm the thunder' is Job 37:4, not 37:3; corrected the citation.
